results.title: Best Practices for Creating Reproducible Experiments in MLOps | by Harshal Shah | Medium
results.content: # Best Practices for Creating Reproducible Experiments in MLOps. Reproducibility in Machine Learning Operations (MLOps) is critical for ensuring reliability and consistency in data-driven experiments. In this article, we will explore some of the best practices that data scientists and machine learning practitioners can implement to create reproducible experiments in MLOps. Version control is fundamental for reproducibility. Implementing a system for tracking and logging experiment details, including hyperparameters, model configurations, evaluation metrics, and training/validation data splits, is another best practice. Using tools like continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipelines to automate model training, evaluation, and deployment processes reduces variability and ensures that experiments can be easily reproduced consistently. Facilitating collaboration and reproducibility by sharing code, data, and trained models with proper documentation is vital. Implementing best practices such as version control, environment management, reproducible data pipelines, experiment tracking, documentation, workflow automation, containerizing models, checkpointing and versioning mechanisms and sharing and collaboration can enhance collaboration, facilitate troubleshooting, and promote the credibility of your work.

results.content: In machine learning, random seeds are critical for ensuring that all operations relying on randomness — such as weight initialization, data shuffling, and dropout — produce the same results across runs. import torchimport numpy as npimport randomdef set_seed(seed): torch.manual_seed(seed) # Sets seed for CPU operations (seed) # Sets seed for NumPy random.seed(seed) # Sets seed for Python's random module if torch.cuda.is_available(): # GPU-specific settings torch.cuda.manual_seed(seed) torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(seed) # If using multiple GPUs .deterministic = True # Ensures deterministic behavior .benchmark = False # Disables non-deterministic optimizations# Example usageset_seed(42). Ensure that data shuffling is consistent across runs by setting random seeds in your data loader. Consistency in initialization, hyperparameters, and hardware settings ensures stable and reproducible results. **Deterministic Mode**: Enforcing deterministic behavior in PyTorch ensures reproducibility across training and inference runs, making it an essential tool for debugging and research. Ensuring consistent and stable training in neural networks goes beyond setting seeds and enabling deterministic behavior. While setting random seeds is a critical step toward reproducibility, ensuring consistent results in machine learning experiments often requires a broader approach. A model trained on one version of PyTorch may yield different results when run on another, even with identical code and data. import torchfrom import DataLoader, Datasetfrom sklearn.model_selection import train_test_splitimport torchvision.transforms as transformsimport numpy as npimport random# Set random seeds for reproducibilitydef set_seed(seed): torch.manual_seed(seed) (seed) random.seed(seed) if torch.cuda.is_available(): torch.cuda.manual_seed(seed) torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(seed) .deterministic = True .benchmark = Falseset_seed(42)# Synthetic datasetclass SyntheticDataset(Dataset): def __init__(self, size=1000, transform=None): self.data = torch.randn(size, 10) # 10 input features self.targets = ((dim=1) > 0).long() # Binary classification self.transform = transform def __len__(self): return len(self.data) def __getitem__(self, idx): sample, target = self.data[idx], self.targets[idx] if self.transform: sample = self.transform(sample) return sample, target# Transformationstransform = transforms.Compose([ transforms.Lambda(lambda x: x + torch.randn_like(x) * 0.01) # Add small noise])# Dataset splitdataset = SyntheticDataset(transform=transform)train_data, val_data = train_test_split(range(len(dataset)), test_size=0.2, random_state=42)train_loader = DataLoader(.Subset(dataset, train_data), batch_size=32, shuffle=True)val_loader = DataLoader(.Subset(dataset, val_data), batch_size=32). **Fixed Data Splits**: Ensure train-test splits are reproducible using a fixed random seed. from pytorch_lightning import seed_everything, Trainerseed_everything(42) # Set seeds for all random number generatorstrainer = Trainer(deterministic=True, max_epochs=10)trainer.fit(model, train_dataloader). Consistency and reproducibility are integral for building trust in machine learning models and ensuring their results can be validated and reused.

results.title: Best Use of Train/Val/Test Splits, with Tips for Medical Data
results.content: Published Time: 2019-09-15T02:41:30+00:00 Best Use of Train/Val/Test Splits, with Tips for Medical Data – Glass Box #### Machine Learning and Medicine, by Rachel Draelos, MD, PhD Best Use of Train/Val/Test Splits, with Tips for Medical Data Date: September 15, 2019Author: Rachel Draelos, MD, PhD This post addresses the appropriate way to split data into a training set, validation set, and test set, and how to use each of these sets to their maximum potential. If you have a tiny training data set your model won’t be able to learn general principles and will have bad validation / test set performance (in other words, it won’t work.) * More validation data is nice because it helps you make a better decision about which model is “The Best.” If you don’t have enough validation data, then there will be a lot of noise in your estimate of which model is “The Best” and you might not make a good choice. This is why for very small data sets, you probably want to use a technique like cross-validation (which is not covered in this post, but if you want to read more about it, you can check out this article.) **Appropriate Use of Train/Validation/Test Data** The key takeaway of this section is the following: YOTO (**Y**ou **O**nly use the **T**est set **O**NCE.) I won’t mince words…If a data scientist wants to develop a new model to solve a problem, and they check the test set performance of a ton of different models and then report the test set performance of the best one, that’s cheating. Once you have decided on one best model – the Most Awesome Model Ever – based on a zillion experiments on your validation data set, it is time to use the test set. didn’t even _create_ a test set until after they were done developing a model using the training and validation data sets. * To train and evaluate a machine learning model, split your data into three sets, for training, validation, and testing.

I want to be able to track the splitting in order to easily retrieve, for example, test and validation sets for integration testing purposes. Registering every intermediate set as different Dataset ? The intra-pipeline artifacts are `PipelineData`, and the inter-pipeline artifacts would be registered Datasets. To actually get actual your question of associating data splits together with a models, our team struggled with this -- especially because for each train,test,split we also have an "extra cols" which contains either identifiers or leaking variables that that the model shouldn't see. In our current ~~hack~~ implementation, we register our "gold" dataset as an Azure ML Dataset at the end of the featurization pipeline. The first step of our training pipline is a `PythonScriptStep`, "Split Data", which contains our train,test,split steps and outputs a pickled dictionary as `data.pkl`. 3") Best Practices for Azure Machine Learning Pipelines. 2") How to organize one step after another in Azure Machine Learning Pipelines?
